curriculum.lesson_evidence: Music is made in every culture and shows what people value and how they live. Steel pans are tuned drums from Trinidad and Tobago, made from steel drums. Taiko are large Japanese drums played with sticks. The djembe is a drum from West Africa played with the hands. Listen to the pieces with respect, find out where and why the music is made and use published, reliable sources. Music from First Nations peoples may have particular protocols, so only use approved recordings and ask local Aboriginal educators for guidance. Never mock or imitate a culture's music.

lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
Choose a piece of music from another culture. Write two respectful things to do before and while listening, and two elements you might describe.

FEEDBACK
Strong answer: 'Find the place and the purpose from a published source, listen quietly to the whole piece. I will describe the tempo and the instruments.' Researching, listening quietly and using music elements show respect.

WATCH FOR
Thinking that all music from a country sounds the same. Each country has many styles and traditions, and learning about one example does not tell you about all of them.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
With an adult, find two pieces from different cultures in a library or on an approved website. For each write the place, the instrument or voice, two elements and a feeling. Write one respectful question you would ask someone from that culture.

Write a short reflection naming one artistic choice you changed and why. Movement or instrument work is optional, adult-supervised and can be described instead.

teach_steps.explain:
Music is made in every culture and shows what people value and how they live. Steel pans are tuned drums from Trinidad and Tobago, made from steel drums. Taiko are large Japanese drums played with sticks. The djembe is a drum from West Africa played with the hands. Music from First Nations peoples may have particular protocols, so only use approved recordings and ask local Aboriginal educators for guidance. Never mock or imitate a culture's music.

This helps the learner make intentional visual, music, drama or dance choices and name their effect, rather than saying an artwork is simply “nice”. Keep every claim linked to an element or technique.
